messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Teacher
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crowding: Crowded places, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Threat: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was thirty-two when it happened, teaching sophomore history at Lincoln High in a neighborhood that had been slowly gentrifying for a decade. He'd always felt safe there—or safe enough. The mugging occurred on a Tuesday evening in October, on the street corner two blocks from the school where he'd stayed late grading papers. A man emerged from a parked car, demanded his wallet, and when Marcus hesitated—a moment of confusion more than resistance—the man shoved him hard against a storefront window. The glass didn't break, but Marcus felt the impact in his spine, the sudden certainty that he was about to be hurt far worse. The attacker grabbed his jacket, wrenched it partway off, and Marcus smelled something acrid and chemical, sweat and cologne mixed with something he couldn't name. There was shouting—he couldn't remember whose voice—and then the man was gone, running. Marcus stood there bleeding from a cut on his forehead, his wallet gone, his body trembling in a way he couldn't control.

The police came. They took a statement, filed a report, and told him they'd look into it. They never called back. Six months later, when Marcus finally asked the precinct about the case, a tired detective told him there was no lead, no suspect, and it would likely remain unsolved. The department was understaffed. These things happened. Marcus felt something calcify inside him then—a recognition that the systems meant to protect him had simply failed, that the world operated on a principle of indifference he'd been naive enough not to see before.

For the first few months after the mugging, Marcus tried to return to normal. He went back to teaching, graded papers at his desk instead of staying late, and told his wife Elena that he was fine. But the world had become a different place. Crowded places—the grocery store on Saturday mornings, the subway platform during rush hour, even his own classroom when all thirty students were present—sent his nervous system into a state of vigilance he couldn't switch off. His heart would accelerate, his palms would sweat, and he found himself studying the faces around him, cataloging expressions, watching for the telltale signs of aggression or intent. Every unexpected movement in his peripheral vision triggered a flood of adrenaline, a primitive conviction that danger was imminent. When a student dropped a textbook in class last spring, Marcus flinched so violently that several kids stared at him in concern.

The memories came without warning, and when they did, they consumed him entirely. He'd be sitting in the faculty lounge or driving home from work when something—a smell, a sudden noise, the particular way someone stood—would crack open the moment, and he was back on that street corner. The chemical smell returned, thick and suffocating. He could taste the copper of his own blood, feel the rough texture of the storefront glass against his palms. The sensations arrived all at once, complete and undeniable, and his mind insisted they were happening now. These intrusions were merciless. They forced their way in unbidden, and no amount of rational effort could stop them. When he was driving with Elena or one of his colleagues, the fear would spike unpredictably—a horn blaring, a car cutting too close—and the memory would surge forward, his body tensing as if the attack were occurring in real time.

The intrusions fed his conviction that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that safety was an illusion. Every time the memory returned with its full sensory weight, it reinforced his belief that threat was everywhere, that he couldn't trust his own assessment of whether a situation was actually safe. And that belief, in turn, made him hypervigilant to new triggers. He began avoiding crowded places deliberately. He stopped going to the grocery store on weekends, stopped attending faculty meetings in the auditorium, stopped taking the subway. When he had to drive with others, his jaw would clench, and he'd find himself scanning exits, mapping routes of escape, watching the other driver's hands on the wheel with an intensity that bordered on obsessive. The more he avoided, the more his threat-detection system seemed to sharpen, as if disuse had honed it into something even more acute. Loud noises became intolerable—he'd wince at the sound of a door slamming, his body flooding with the conviction that violence was about to erupt.

Elena noticed the withdrawal. She noticed that he'd stopped suggesting they go out to dinner, that he'd declined invitations to his department's holiday party, that he spent his evenings at home with the doors locked and the windows checked. She didn't understand why he couldn't just move past it, why he seemed to be getting worse rather than better as the months accumulated. Marcus couldn't explain to her, or to himself, why the injustice of it—the fact that his attacker had never been found, that the police had done nothing, that he alone was left to carry the consequences—seemed to deepen his sense that the world operated without fairness or accountability. That unfairness, that institutional abandonment, had become woven into his understanding of reality itself. When the memory forced its way in, he didn't just relive the attack; he relived the betrayal of having asked for help and received none.

It's been six years now, and Marcus is here because Elena gave him an ultimatum. She loves him, she said, but she can't watch him disappear. He's forty-two now, still teaching, but he's stopped sponsoring the debate team because he can't manage the trips. He's stopped going to faculty social events. He avoids the grocery store and orders everything online. The world has contracted to a set of safe spaces and predictable routines, and anything that threatens that containment sends him into a state of dread he can barely articulate. What frightens him most is that he's become someone he doesn't recognize—someone ruled by fear, someone whose mind betrays him with memories he can't control, someone who believes, with a certainty that feels unshakeable, that the systems meant to protect people are hollow and that danger is the only truth.
